lesson.title: What Exactly Gets Applied? Defining Treatment in an Experiment
lesson.summary: A treatment is the specific, precisely defined condition that researchers impose on an experimental unit, and vague or inconsistent treatment definitions undermine an experiment before a single measurement is taken.
lesson.body:
A treatment is the specific condition that researchers impose on an experimental unit in an experiment. It is the thing being tested, the exact combination of conditions a unit experiences, and it is what separates one experimental group from another. In the fertilizer experiment from earlier, the two treatments were the new fertilizer and the standard fertilizer, each applied to 20 plots.

Every experiment exists to compare the effects of different treatments on the response variable, so defining the treatments precisely is one of the first and most important steps in designing a study. A vague treatment description, such as give some students extra help, is not usable in an experiment because it cannot be applied consistently to every unit assigned to it. A usable treatment description is specific and repeatable, such as a 30 minute one-on-one tutoring session twice per week for four weeks, so that every unit assigned to that treatment genuinely receives the same thing.

It helps to keep treatment separate from two related ideas it is easy to confuse it with. The response variable is what gets measured after the treatment is applied, such as bushels per acre or exam score, and it is not itself the treatment. And a condition that withholds the substance under study, such as no fertilizer at all, still counts as one of the treatments being compared, since it is still a specific, deliberately assigned condition, not an accident of which plots happened to go untreated.

Consider a study testing whether a new fertilizer's effect depends on the amount applied. Researchers might define three treatments: no fertilizer, 5 pounds of fertilizer per plot, and 10 pounds of fertilizer per plot. If 15 plots are randomly split into three groups of 5, each group receiving one of the three treatments, and the average yields come out to 140, 156, and 171 bushels per acre respectively across the three groups, the treatments are precisely what makes the three groups comparable, since every plot within a treatment group received exactly the same fertilizer amount and every other growing condition was held constant.

When an experiment varies more than one thing at once, such as fertilizer amount and watering frequency together, statisticians break the treatment down further into factors, the individual explanatory variables being manipulated, and levels, the specific values or categories each factor takes. A single treatment in a multi-factor experiment is really a specific combination of one level from each factor, an idea the next two sections build out fully.

Because the treatment is the one thing that is supposed to differ systematically between experimental groups, sloppy treatment definitions undermine an experiment before a single measurement is even taken. If the new fertilizer group secretly also received more careful watering, the resulting yield difference could no longer be cleanly attributed to fertilizer alone.
